source_text: Cetera aeque animi impedimenta usque ad limen carceris deduxerint vos, quousque et parentes vestri. Exinde segregati estis ab ipso mundo, quanto magis a saeculo rebusque eius? Nec hoc vos consternet, quod segregati estis a mundo. Si enim recogitemus ipsum magis mundum carcerem esse, exisse vos e carcere quam in carcerem introisse intellegemus. Maiores tenebras habet mundus, quae hominum praecordia excaecant. Graviores catenas induit mundus, quae ipsas animas hominum constringunt. Peiores immunditias expirat mundus, libidines hominum. Plures postremo mundus reos continet, scilicet universum hominum genus. Iudicia denique non proconsulis, sed dei sustinet. Quo vos, benedicti, de carcere in custodiarium, si forte, translatos existimetis. Habet tenebras, sed lumen estis ipsi. Habet vincula, sed vos soluti deo estis. Triste illic expirat, sed vos odor estis suavitatis. Iudex expectatur, sed vos estis de iudicibus ipsis iudicaturi. Contristetur illi qui fructum saeculi suspirat. Christianus etiam extra carcerem saeculo renuntiavit, in carcere autem etiam carceri. Nihil interest, ubi sitis in saeculo, qui extra saeculum estis. Et si aliqua amisistis vitae gaudia, negotiatio est aliquid amittere, ut maiora lucreris. Nihil adhuc dico de praemio, ad quod deus martyres invitat. Ipsam interim conversationem saeculi et carceris comparemus, si non plus in carcere spiritus acquirit, quam caro amittit. Immo et quae iusta sunt caro non amittit per curam ecclesiae et agapen fratrum, et insuper quae semper utilia fidei, spiritus adipiscitur. Non vides alienos deos, non imaginibus eorum incurris, non sollemnes nationum dies ipsa commixtione participas, non nidoribus spurcis verberaris, non clamoribus spectaculorum, atrocitate vel furore vel impudicitia celebrantium caederis, non in loca libidinum publicarum oculi tui impingunt, vacas a scandalis, a temptationibus, a recordationibus malis, iam et a persecutione. Hoc praestat carcer Christiano, quod eremus prophetis. Ipse dominus in secessu frequentius agebat, ut liberius oraret, ut saeculo cederet: gloriam denique suam discipulis in solitudine demonstravit. Auferamus carceris nomen, secessum vocemus. Etsi corpus includitur, etsi caro detinetur, omnia spiritui patent. Vagare spiritu, spatiare spiritu et non stadia opaca aut porticus longas proponens tibi, sed illam viam, quae ad deum ducit. Quotiens eam spiritu deambulaveris, totiens in carcere non eris. Nihil crus sentit in nervo, cum animus in caelo est. Totum hominem animus circumfert et, quo velit, transfert. Ubi autem erit cor tuum, illic erit et thesaurus tuus. Ibi ergo sit cor nostrum, ubi volumus habere thesaurum.
thought_title: The prison as retreat from the world
orientation: Tertullian is addressing the imprisoned Christians, arguing that their prison is not a loss but a spiritual retreat, since the world itself is a worse prison.
pass_a_gloss: The other equally [great] hindrances of the mind may have led you as far as the threshold of the prison, as far as also your parents [did]. From then on you have been separated from the world itself, how much more from the world and its affairs? And let this not dismay you, that you have been separated from the world. For if we should consider that the world itself is more [truly] a prison, we will understand that you have gone out of a prison rather than entered into a prison. The world has greater darknesses, which blind the hearts of men. The world puts on heavier chains, which bind the very souls of men. The world breathes out worse filths, the lusts of men. Finally the world contains more guilty persons, namely the whole human race. In short it undergoes the judgments not of a proconsul, but of God. Therefore, blessed ones, consider yourselves transferred from a prison into a guardhouse, if perhaps [that is the case]. It has darknesses, but you yourselves are light. It has chains, but you are loosed for God. It breathes out sadness there, but you are an odor of sweetness. A judge is awaited, but you are going to judge the judges themselves. Let him be saddened who longs for the fruit of the world. A Christian even outside prison has renounced the world, but in prison he has renounced even the prison. It matters nothing where you are in the world, you who are outside the world. And if you have lost some joys of life, it is a business transaction to lose something, so that you may gain greater things. I say nothing yet about the reward, to which God invites the martyrs. Let us meanwhile compare the very manner of life of the world and of the prison, [to see] if the spirit does not acquire more in prison than the flesh loses. Nay rather, the flesh does not lose even the things that are rightfully [its own], through the care of the church and the love of the brothers, and in addition the spirit obtains the things that are always useful to faith. You do not see foreign gods, you do not run into their images, you do not share in the solemn days of the nations by the very mixing [with them], you are not struck by foul smells, you are not cut by the shouts of the spectacles, by the atrocity or fury or shamelessness of those celebrating, your eyes do not strike against places of public lusts, you are free from scandals, from temptations, from evil recollections, now even from persecution. The prison provides this to a Christian, which the desert [provided] to the prophets. The Lord himself acted in retreat more frequently, so that he might pray more freely, so that he might withdraw from the world: in short he showed his glory to his disciples in solitude. Let us take away the name of prison, let us call it a retreat. Even if the body is shut in, even if the flesh is detained, all things are open to the spirit. Wander in spirit, walk about in spirit, setting before yourself not shady porticoes or long colonnades, but that way which leads to God. As often as you walk along it in spirit, so often you will not be in prison. The leg feels nothing in the fetter, when the mind is in heaven. The mind carries the whole man around and transfers him wherever it wishes. But where your heart will be, there also will be your treasure. Therefore let our heart be there, where we wish to have our treasure.

choices.why: Tertullian contrasts the prison (carcer) with a lighter form of custody; 'guardhouse' preserves the military/penal nuance without implying a worse place.

choices.english: it is a business transaction to lose something
choices.why: The commercial metaphor is deliberate: losing earthly joys is an exchange that yields greater profit. 'Business transaction' keeps the mercantile force.
rejected: it is a bargain to lose something
it is a trade to lose something

choices.why: The phrase echoes 2 Corinthians 2:15 imagery; 'sweet fragrance' renders the genitive of quality naturally while keeping the sensory contrast with the prison's bad smell.

choices.english: let us call it a retreat
choices.why: The glossary requires 'retreat' for secessus; the verb vocemus is hortatory subjunctive, so 'let us call' preserves the communal exhortation.
rejected: we should call it a retreat
let it be called a retreat

choices.why: Vacare with a/ab means to be free from or unoccupied by; 'you are free from' captures the release from moral dangers.

choices.english: you are not struck by foul smells
choices.why: Verberaris is passive of verbero, to beat or strike; the image is of being assaulted by smells. 'Struck by' keeps the violence of the verb.
rejected: you are not beaten by foul smells
you are not lashed by foul smells

bible_refs.note: Ubi autem erit cor tuum, illic erit et thesaurus tuus

pass_b_english: The other hindrances of the mind have accompanied you as far as the prison threshold, just as your relatives have. From that point you have been separated from the world itself—how much more from its affairs and concerns? Do not let this disturb you, that you have been separated from the world. If we reflect that the world itself is more truly a prison, we will understand that you have gone out of a prison rather than entered into one. The world has greater darkness, which blinds the hearts of men. The world wears heavier chains, which bind the very souls of men. The world breathes out worse filth—the lusts of men. Finally, the world holds more prisoners: the entire human race. And it awaits judgment not from a proconsul, but from God. Consider yourselves, blessed ones, to have been transferred from prison to a guardhouse, if anything. It has darkness, but you yourselves are light. It has chains, but you are free before God. It breathes out gloom, but you are a sweet fragrance. A judge is awaited, but you will be judges of the judges themselves. Let the one who longs for the fruit of the world grieve. A Christian has renounced the world even outside prison; in prison he has renounced even the prison itself. It makes no difference where you are in the world, since you are outside the world. And if you have lost some of life's pleasures, it is a business transaction to lose something so that you may gain greater things. I say nothing yet of the prize to which God invites martyrs. Let us compare for the moment the life of the world and the life of prison: if the spirit does not gain more in prison than the flesh loses. Indeed, the flesh does not lose what is rightfully its own, through the care of the church and the love of the brothers; and beyond that, the spirit obtains what is always useful for faith. You do not see foreign gods, you do not run into their images, you do not share in the festival days of the nations by mixing with them, you are not struck by foul smells, you are not cut by the shouts of the spectacles—by the cruelty or frenzy or shamelessness of those celebrating—your eyes do not fall upon places of public lust. You are free from scandals, from temptations, from evil memories, and now even from persecution. The prison gives the Christian what the desert gave the prophets. The Lord himself often acted in retreat, so that he might pray more freely and withdraw from the world; indeed, he showed his glory to his disciples in solitude. Let us take away the name of prison and call it a retreat. Even if the body is shut in, even if the flesh is held, all things are open to the spirit. Wander in spirit, walk about in spirit—and do not set before yourself shaded colonnades or long porticoes, but that road which leads to God. As often as you walk along it in spirit, so often you will not be in prison. The leg feels nothing in the shackle when the mind is in heaven. The mind carries the whole person about and transfers him wherever it wishes. Where your heart will be, there your treasure will be also (Matthew 6:21). Therefore let our heart be there, where we wish to have our treasure.

last_rejected.why: 'Nidoribus spurcis' means foul-smelling smoke or fumes, not smells; 'verberaris' means beaten/struck.
last_rejected.fix: you are not battered by foul fumes
last_rejected.ruling: source 'non nidoribus spurcis verberaris' = not struck by filthy smells; translation matches

last_rejected.quote: The prison gives the Christian what the desert gave the prophets.
last_rejected.source_quote: Hoc praestat carcer Christiano, quod eremus prophetis.
last_rejected.why: Latin says the prison benefits the Christian, not the desert.
last_rejected.fix: The prison gives the Christian what the prison gave the prophets.
last_rejected.ruling: English correctly renders 'Hoc praestat carcer...quod eremus': prison provides what desert provided. No desert-as-subject error.

last_rejected.quote: The leg feels nothing in the shackle when the mind is in heaven.
last_rejected.source_quote: Nihil crus sentit in nervo, cum animus in caelo est.
last_rejected.why: Latin says the leg feels nothing in the nerve, not a shackle.
last_rejected.fix: The leg feels nothing in the nerve when the mind is in heaven.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Nervus' means sinew/nerve but also shackle/bond; 'in nervo' = in the shackle. Standard lexical range, not a mistranslation.
